strings.name: Salman Rushdie
strings.country: United Kingdom / United States; born in India
strings.summary: Born in Bombay and educated in Britain, Rushdie combines exaggeration, allegory and many-voiced narratives with history and migration. Midnight’s Children entwines individual lives with post-independence India. The Satanic Verses prompted bans, death threats and debates about expression. He continued writing and speaking publicly. After surviving a 2022 stabbing, he documented recovery in Knife and returned to fiction with The Eleventh Hour.
strings.coverageNote: Research cutoff: 2026-11-13. Selected milestones span 1947–2026; this is not a complete catalogue or live news archive.
strings.influence.rationale: Combined history and imagination in novels including Midnight's Children; his writing and life became important subjects in migrant literature and debates over free expression.
strings.facts.fact-01.label: Birthplace
strings.facts.fact-01.value: Bombay, British India; now Mumbai, India
strings.facts.fact-02.label: Education
strings.facts.fact-02.value: History, King’s College, Cambridge; graduated in 1968
strings.highlights.highlight-01.title: History intertwined with fantasy
strings.highlights.highlight-01.text: Midnight’s Children connects family narrative with post-independence India; it won the 1981 Booker and later anniversary awards.
strings.highlights.highlight-02.title: A continuing debate about expression
strings.highlights.highlight-02.text: Controversy and threats surrounding The Satanic Verses, and his subsequent writing, sustain debates about migrant identity and freedom of expression.
strings.timeline.event-01.title: Appears on PBS Firing Line
strings.timeline.event-01.text: He discussed life after the attack, returning to writing and the public circumstances of literature, religious threats and expression.
strings.timeline.event-02.title: Publishes The Eleventh Hour
strings.timeline.event-02.text: Five works of fiction move between India, Britain and America, examining late life, legacy, death and identity.
strings.timeline.event-03.title: Publishes Knife
strings.timeline.event-03.text: The memoir recounts the 2022 attack and recovery, connecting trauma with love, art and the continuation of life.
strings.timeline.event-04.title: Survives a stabbing at a public event
strings.timeline.event-04.text: He was attacked before a lecture in Chautauqua, New York, survived severe injuries and gradually recovered while continuing to write.
strings.timeline.event-05.title: Faces a death decree over The Satanic Verses
strings.timeline.event-05.text: Ayatollah Khomeini’s decree forced him into protected life and intensified international debates about freedom of expression.
strings.timeline.event-06.title: Publishes The Satanic Verses
strings.timeline.event-06.text: The novel explores migration, transformation and religious imagination; publication prompted controversy, bans and violence against people associated with it.
strings.timeline.event-07.title: Midnight’s Children wins the Booker
strings.timeline.event-07.text: Characters born at independence link personal memory with national history, establishing a major place for his work in English fiction.
strings.timeline.event-08.title: Publishes Grimus
strings.timeline.event-08.text: His first novel combined fantasy and science fiction, beginning continuing experiments with myth, identity and narrative form.
strings.timeline.event-09.title: Graduates from Cambridge
strings.timeline.event-09.text: After studying history at King’s College, he worked in London and gradually transformed historical interests into fiction.
strings.timeline.event-10.title: Born in Bombay
strings.timeline.event-10.text: Born shortly before Indian independence, he later studied in Britain; this cross-cultural upbringing became an important context for his fiction.
